sections.title: The three states and the tug-of-war behind them

board_events.text: States of matter: solid, liquid, gas
Matter = anything that has mass and occupies space.
Solid: fixed shape and volume. Liquid: fixed volume, no fixed shape. Gas: neither.
One substance, three costumes: ice, water, steam.
Two things compete: how strongly particles attract, and their thermal energy of motion.
Solid: attractions win, particles only vibrate in place.
Liquid: the two are comparable, particles stay close but slide past one another.
Gas: thermal motion dominates, particles fly apart and fill any container.
Heating loosens attractions, so heat pushes matter solid to liquid to gas.

segments.text: <curious>Let's begin at the very beginning. What exactly is matter?
Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space, the phone in your hand, the air you breathe, the water on your table.
It comes in three states. A solid holds its shape and volume, like a piece of chalk. A liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container. A gas has neither.
And notice, the same substance can wear all three costumes. Ice, water and steam are one substance at three temperatures.
So what actually decides the state? A tug of war between two things: how strongly the particles attract each other, and how much thermal energy they have to move.
In a solid, the attractions win. The particles can only vibrate in fixed positions, so the shape and volume stay fixed.
In a liquid, the two forces are comparable. Particles stay close but flow past one another, giving fixed volume but no fixed shape.
In a gas, thermal motion dominates completely. Particles fly apart and fill whatever container they are in, and they compress easily.
That is why heating matters. Heat supplies energy that loosens the attractions, pushing matter from solid to liquid to gas.
<curious>चलो बिल्कुल शुरू से शुरू करते हैं। Matter आखिर होता क्या है?
Matter का मतलब है कोई भी ऐसी चीज़ जिसमें mass हो और जो space घेरे, आपका phone, breathe करने वाली air, table पर रखा water.
ये तीन states में आता है। Solid अपनी shape और volume दोनों रखता है, जैसे chalk का टुकड़ा। Liquid का volume fixed रहता है पर shape container की। Gas में दोनों नहीं।
और देखो, एक ही substance तीनों costume पहन सकता है। Ice, water और steam एक ही चीज़ हैं तीन अलग temperature पर।
तो state decide कौन करता है? दो चीज़ों की tug of war: particles एक दूसरे को कितना attract करते हैं, और उनके पास move करने की कितनी thermal energy है।
Solid में attractions जीत जाते हैं। Particles सिर्फ़ fixed जगह पर vibrate करते हैं, इसलिए shape और volume fixed रहते हैं।
Liquid में दोनों forces बराबर हैं। Particles पास तो रहते हैं पर एक दूसरे के ऊपर से slide करते हैं, इसलिए volume fixed पर shape नहीं।
Gas में thermal motion पूरी तरह हावी हो जाती है। Particles बिखर जाते हैं और पूरा container भर देते हैं, और आसानी से compress हो जाते हैं।
इसीलिए heating मायने रखती है। Heat वो energy देती है जो attractions को ढीला करके matter को solid से liquid, फिर gas तक धकेलती है।

sections.title: Pure substances versus mixtures: the master tree

board_events.text: First question: is the composition fixed or free?
Pure substance: fixed composition, cannot be split by physical means.
Element: only one kind of atom, like gold, iron, oxygen.
Compound: two or more elements chemically bonded in a fixed mass ratio, like water, salt.
Mixture: substances physically blended in any proportion, each keeping its own identity.
Homogeneous: uniform throughout, like salt water, air, brass.
Heterogeneous: visibly distinct regions, like sand and iron filings.

board_events.text: Salt is a compound, not a mixture: no sieve, magnet or filter separates Na from Cl.

segments.text: The deeper sorting asks one question: is this one kind of stuff, or several mixed together?
If the composition is fixed and you cannot separate it by physical means, it is a pure substance.
Pure substances split in two. An element is made of only one kind of atom, gold, iron, oxygen.
A compound is two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio by mass, like water or common salt. That fixed ratio is the law of definite proportions you will meet soon.
A mixture is different: two or more substances physically blended in any proportion, and each one keeps its own identity.
Mixtures split too. A homogeneous mixture is uniform throughout, you cannot see boundaries, think salt water, air, or brass.
A heterogeneous mixture has visibly distinct regions, sand and iron filings, oil and water, a fruit salad.
Here is the whole family on one tree, matter branching into pure substances and mixtures, and each of those into two.

One warning that traps students: common salt is a compound, not a mixture. Its sodium and chlorine are chemically bonded, so no sieve, magnet or filter can pull them apart, only a chemical reaction can.
अगली, गहरी sorting एक सवाल पूछती है: ये एक ही तरह का stuff है, या कई चीज़ें mix हैं?
अगर composition fixed है और physical तरीक़ों से अलग नहीं कर सकते, तो वो pure substance है।
Pure substances दो में बँटते हैं। Element सिर्फ़ एक तरह के atom का बना होता है, gold, iron, oxygen.
Compound में दो या ज़्यादा elements chemically combine होते हैं fixed mass ratio में, जैसे water या common salt. यही fixed ratio law of definite proportions है जो आगे मिलेगा।
Mixture अलग है: दो या ज़्यादा substances physically mix होते हैं किसी भी proportion में, और हर एक अपनी identity रखता है।
Mixtures भी बँटते हैं। Homogeneous mixture हर जगह uniform होता है, boundaries दिखती नहीं, जैसे salt water, air, या brass.
Heterogeneous mixture में साफ़ अलग regions दिखते हैं, sand और iron filings, oil और water, एक fruit salad.
ये देखो पूरा family एक tree पर, matter बँटता है pure substances और mixtures में, और हर एक आगे दो में।

एक warning जो students को फँसाती है: common salt एक compound है, mixture नहीं। इसका sodium और chlorine chemically bonded हैं, इसलिए कोई sieve, magnet या filter इन्हें अलग नहीं कर सकता, सिर्फ़ chemical reaction कर सकती है।

sections.title: Physical versus chemical, and the classification routine

board_events.text: Physical or chemical? Ask: is a NEW substance formed?
Physical property: observed without changing identity, colour, melting point, density.
Chemical property: describes forming new substances, combustibility, reactivity with water.
Physical change: no new substance, usually reversible, melting, dissolving, tearing.
Chemical change: new substance with new properties, burning, rusting, curdling.
Dissolving salt is physical: evaporate the water and get the salt back.
Classify matter: (1) fixed or variable composition? (2) one substance or many bonded?
That physical methods alone separate a sample is itself proof it was a mixture.

segments.text: Matter is also described by its properties, and this gives us the single sharpest question in the whole subtopic: was a new substance formed?
A physical property can be seen without changing what the substance is, colour, melting point, boiling point, density, solubility.
A chemical property describes how a substance turns into new substances, combustibility, acidity, reactivity with water.
That distinction drives change. A physical change makes no new substance and is usually reversible, melting ice, dissolving sugar, tearing paper.
A chemical change forms a new substance with new properties and is usually not easily reversed, burning paper, rusting iron, curdling milk.
Watch this one carefully. Dissolving salt feels like something new is made, but it is physical, evaporate the water and the salt comes right back.
For classifying any sample, run a clean routine. First ask, is the composition fixed or variable? Then, if pure, is it one substance or many chemically bonded?
And here is a lovely idea: the very fact that physical methods alone can separate a sample is the proof that it was a mixture, never a compound.
Matter को उसकी properties से भी describe करते हैं, और यहीं से मिलता है पूरे subtopic का सबसे तेज़ सवाल: कोई नया substance बना क्या?
Physical property वो है जो substance की identity बदले बिना देखी जा सके, colour, melting point, boiling point, density, solubility.
Chemical property बताती है कि substance कैसे नए substances में बदलता है, combustibility, acidity, water के साथ reactivity.
यही distinction change को चलाती है। Physical change में कोई नया substance नहीं बनता और आमतौर पर reversible होता है, ice melt होना, sugar dissolve होना, paper फटना।
Chemical change में नया substance नई properties के साथ बनता है और आसानी से reverse नहीं होता, paper जलना, iron rust होना, milk फटना।
इसे ध्यान से देखो। Salt dissolve करना लगता है जैसे कुछ नया बना, पर ये physical है, water evaporate करो और salt वापस आ जाता है।
किसी भी sample को classify करने के लिए एक साफ़ routine चलाओ। पहले पूछो, composition fixed है या variable? फिर, अगर pure है, तो एक substance है या कई chemically bonded?
और ये एक सुंदर idea है: यही बात कि सिर्फ़ physical methods sample को अलग कर देते हैं, यही proof है कि वो mixture था, compound कभी नहीं।

sections.title: Classifying elements, compounds and mixtures

board_events.text: Classify: brass, ozone (O₃), baking soda (NaHCO₃), sea water
Brass: copper and zinc in variable proportion, uniform → homogeneous mixture.
Ozone, O₃: one atom type only (oxygen) → element.
Baking soda: Na, H, C, O bonded in a fixed ratio → compound.
Sea water: water plus dissolved salts, variable, uniform → homogeneous mixture.
Which is NOT a mixture? air, gasoline, diamond, bronze
Diamond is pure carbon, a single element → the odd one out.
Ignore looks. Ask only: how many kinds of substance?

segments.text: Let's turn the routine into reflex with a board favourite. Classify each as element, compound, or mixture.
Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, mixed in variable proportion and uniform to the eye, so it is a homogeneous mixture.
Ozone, written O three, is built from a single kind of atom, oxygen only, so it is an element.
Baking soda has sodium, hydrogen, carbon and oxygen chemically combined in a fixed ratio, that is a compound.
Sea water is water with dissolved salts in variable amount, uniform in appearance, so it is a homogeneous mixture. Each time the deciding question is fixed or variable, one atom type or many bonded.
<chuckle>Now a classic speed trap. Which of these is not a mixture, air, gasoline, diamond, or bronze?
Diamond is pure carbon, a single element. Air is a mix of gases, gasoline a mix of hydrocarbons, bronze a copper tin alloy, all mixtures. So diamond is the answer.
The lesson stares back at you: ignore how it looks, and ask only how many kinds of substance are present.
इस routine को reflex बनाते हैं एक board favourite से। हर एक को classify करो, element, compound, या mixture.
Brass copper और zinc का alloy है, variable proportion में mixed और आँख को uniform, तो ये homogeneous mixture है।
Ozone, यानी O three, सिर्फ़ एक तरह के atom से बना है, केवल oxygen, तो ये element है।
Baking soda में sodium, hydrogen, carbon और oxygen fixed ratio में chemically combined हैं, वो compound है।
Sea water water है dissolved salts के साथ variable amount में, दिखने में uniform, तो homogeneous mixture. हर बार deciding सवाल वही, fixed या variable, एक atom type या कई bonded.
<chuckle>अब एक classic speed trap. इनमें mixture कौन नहीं है, air, gasoline, diamond, या bronze?
Diamond pure carbon है, एक single element. Air gases का mix, gasoline hydrocarbons का mix, bronze copper tin alloy, ये सब mixtures हैं। तो answer है diamond.
Lesson सामने ही है: कैसा दिखता है ये भूल जाओ, बस पूछो कितनी तरह के substance मौजूद हैं।

sections.title: Physical or chemical change, and the copper sulphate trap

board_events.text: Physical or chemical change?
Sublimation of camphor: solid to vapour, same substance → physical.
Souring of milk: lactose becomes lactic acid, a new substance → chemical.
Dissolving sugar in tea: recoverable by evaporation → physical.
Digestion: large molecules broken into new smaller ones → chemical.
The one test: was a new substance formed?
JEE edge case: dissolving anhydrous CuSO₄
White CuSO₄ in water turns blue, forming hydrated CuSO₄·5H₂O, with heat released.
Colour change + heat = a chemical step hiding inside the dissolving.

segments.text: Now let's practise the change test with four everyday processes.
Sublimation of camphor is solid turning to vapour, still the same substance, so physical.
Souring of milk converts lactose into lactic acid, a genuinely new substance, so chemical.
Dissolving sugar in tea is physical, the sugar can be recovered by evaporation, no new substance.
Digestion breaks large molecules into new, smaller ones by reactions, so it is chemical.
See how one test settles all four, was a new substance formed? State changes and dissolving are physical, anything making new compounds is chemical.
<whisper>Now the edge case J E E Advanced loves. A student claims dissolving white anhydrous copper sulphate is purely physical, just like salt.
But in water it turns blue, forming hydrated copper sulphate, that dot five water species, and it releases heat. A chemically distinct, coloured substance has appeared.
So the claim is not fully correct. The bulk dissolving is physical, but the colour change and the heat reveal a real chemical step, hydration. Those two signs are your warning flags.
अब change test को चार रोज़मर्रा के processes पर practise करते हैं।
Camphor का sublimation solid से vapour बनना है, substance वही है, तो physical.
Milk का sour होना lactose को lactic acid में बदल देता है, एक सचमुच नया substance, तो chemical.
Tea में sugar dissolve करना physical है, sugar evaporation से वापस मिल जाती है, कोई नया substance नहीं।
Digestion बड़ी molecules को reactions से नई, छोटी molecules में तोड़ता है, तो ये chemical है।
देखो एक ही test चारों को settle कर देता है, नया substance बना क्या? State changes और dissolving physical, नए compounds बनाना chemical.
<whisper>अब वो edge case जो J E E Advanced को बहुत पसंद है। एक student कहता है white anhydrous copper sulphate dissolve करना purely physical है, बिलकुल salt जैसा।
पर water में ये blue हो जाता है, hydrated copper sulphate बनाता है, वो dot five water वाला, और heat release करता है। एक chemically अलग, coloured substance आ गया।
तो claim पूरी तरह सही नहीं। Bulk dissolving physical है, पर colour change और heat एक असली chemical step दिखाते हैं, hydration. यही दो signs आपके warning flags हैं।

sections.title: Classification pitfalls and the two-question filter

board_events.text: Traps when classifying matter
Homogeneous mixture vs compound: both look uniform, but a compound has fixed composition and needs chemical separation.
Never classify by appearance: diamond and graphite are both carbon; brass and copper both look metallic.
Dissolving is usually physical, but coloured hydration or gas evolution signals chemistry.
Dramatic is not chemical: boiling, sublimation and shattering are all physical.
Pro-tip: run the two-question filter, fixed or variable, then one substance or many.
Those two questions resolve almost every element-compound-mixture item in seconds.

segments.text: Let's lock in the traps so they never cost you a mark.
First, confusing a homogeneous mixture with a compound. Both look uniform, but a compound has a fixed composition and needs chemical separation, while a mixture varies and separates physically.
Second, classifying by appearance. Diamond and graphite look nothing alike yet are both carbon, and brass and copper both look metallic yet one is a mixture. Judge by composition, never by looks.
Third, calling dissolving chemical. It is usually physical, but watch for genuine exceptions, a coloured hydration or gas bubbling off, which do signal chemistry.
Fourth, equating dramatic with chemical. Boiling, sublimation and shattering all look dramatic yet stay physical, because no new substance forms.
<excited>Here is the pro-tip that wins these fast. Silently run a two-question filter, first fixed or variable composition, then one substance or many.
Those two questions, with appearance ignored entirely, resolve almost every classification item in a few seconds.
इन traps को पक्का कर लेते हैं ताकि कभी एक mark भी न जाए।

पहला, homogeneous mixture को compound समझ लेना। दोनों uniform दिखते हैं, पर compound की composition fixed होती है और उसे chemical separation चाहिए, जबकि mixture vary करता है और physically अलग होता है।

दूसरा, appearance से classify करना। Diamond और graphite बिलकुल अलग दिखते हैं फिर भी दोनों carbon हैं, और brass और copper दोनों metallic दिखते हैं फिर भी एक mixture है। Composition से judge करो, looks से कभी नहीं।
तीसरा, dissolving को chemical कहना। ये आमतौर पर physical है, पर genuine exceptions पर नज़र रखो, coloured hydration या gas निकलना, जो chemistry का इशारा देते हैं।
चौथा, dramatic को chemical मान लेना। Boiling, sublimation और shattering dramatic दिखते हैं फिर भी physical रहते हैं, क्योंकि कोई नया substance नहीं बनता।
<excited>अब वो pro-tip जो इन्हें तेज़ी से जिता देता है। मन में एक two-question filter चलाओ, पहले fixed या variable composition, फिर एक substance या कई।
ये दो सवाल, appearance को पूरी तरह ignore करके, लगभग हर classification item को कुछ ही seconds में हल कर देते हैं।

sections.title: Why every quantity needs a unit, and the seven SI base units

board_events.text: Quantity = number × unit
A bare number is meaningless: 5 of what — grams, kilograms, sacks?
The SI system fixes seven base units for seven fundamental quantities.
Length → metre (m), mass → kilogram (kg), time → second (s).
Current → ampere (A), temperature → kelvin (K).
Amount of substance → mole (mol), luminous intensity → candela (cd).
Everything else is derived: area m², volume m³, speed m s⁻¹.
Density = mass per volume: kg m⁻³, or lab-friendly g cm⁻³.

segments.text: <curious>Imagine telling a shopkeeper you want five of sugar. Five what?
A bare number is meaningless in science. Every physical quantity is a number times a unit, five kilograms, not just five. The number says how many, the unit says how many of what.
To stop everyone inventing their own units, scientists agreed on the S I system, built on seven base units, each measuring one fundamental quantity.
Length is measured in the metre, mass in the kilogram, and time in the second.
Electric current is measured in the ampere, and temperature in the kelvin.
Amount of substance is measured in the mole, and luminous intensity in the candela. Seven quantities, seven base units.
Everything else is a derived unit built from these. Area is metre squared, volume is metre cubed, speed is metre per second.
Density is a favourite derived quantity, mass per unit volume, in kilogram per metre cubed, or the lab-friendly gram per centimetre cubed.
<curious>सोचो आप shopkeeper से कहते हो, मुझे sugar का पाँच चाहिए। पाँच क्या?
Science में bare number बेमतलब है। हर physical quantity एक number गुणा एक unit है, पाँच kilogram, सिर्फ़ पाँच नहीं। Number बताता है कितने, unit बताता है किसके कितने।
ताकि हर कोई अपनी unit न बनाए, scientists ने S I system पर सहमति बनाई, सात base units पर बना, हर एक एक fundamental quantity नापता है।
Length metre में नापी जाती है, mass kilogram में, और time second में।
Electric current ampere में नापते हैं, और temperature kelvin में।
Amount of substance mole में नापते हैं, और luminous intensity candela में। सात quantities, सात base units.
बाक़ी सब इनसे बने derived units हैं। Area है metre squared, volume metre cubed, speed metre per second.
Density एक favourite derived quantity है, mass प्रति volume, kilogram per metre cubed में, या lab में आसान gram per centimetre cubed में।

sections.title: Prefixes, factor-label, mass vs weight, and temperature scales

board_events.text: Prefixes scale a unit by powers of ten
kilo 10³, centi 10⁻², milli 10⁻³.
micro 10⁻⁶, nano 10⁻⁹, pico 10⁻¹².
Units are like currencies; prefixes like denominations.
Factor-label: multiply by a fraction equal to 1 so the unwanted unit cancels.
Mass is the amount of matter (kg) and never changes.
Weight is the gravitational force, $W=mg$ (newton), and changes with location.
Temperature: Celsius everyday, Kelvin the SI absolute scale, Fahrenheit in a few places.
Kelvin never goes negative; a negative K is a sure sign of error.

segments.text: Because a metre is sometimes too big or too small, S I uses prefixes that scale a unit up or down in powers of ten.
kilo is ten to the three, centi is ten to the minus two, and milli is ten to the minus three.
micro is ten to the minus six, nano ten to the minus nine, and pico ten to the minus twelve, the scale of single molecules.
Think of units as currencies and prefixes as denominations. Two thousand metres is like two thousand rupees, two kilometres is like two thousand-rupee notes, same value, tidier.
And converting units uses the factor-label method, multiply by a fraction equal to one, like one kilogram over one thousand grams, so the unwanted unit cancels and the wanted one survives.
Two ideas trip students. Mass is the amount of matter, measured in kilograms, and it never changes.
Weight is the gravitational force on that mass, W equals m g, measured in newton, and it changes with location, less on a mountaintop, far less on the Moon.
And temperature comes in three scales, Celsius for everyday life, Kelvin the S I absolute scale, and Fahrenheit used in a few countries.
One rule to burn in: Kelvin never goes negative. A negative kelvin temperature is a sure sign that an error crept in.
क्योंकि metre कभी बहुत बड़ा तो कभी बहुत छोटा होता है, S I prefixes इस्तेमाल करता है जो unit को powers of ten में ऊपर नीचे scale करते हैं।
kilo है ten to the three, centi है ten to the minus two, और milli है ten to the minus three.
micro है ten to the minus six, nano ten to the minus nine, और pico ten to the minus twelve, single molecules का scale.
Units को currencies समझो और prefixes को denominations. दो हज़ार metres दो हज़ार rupees जैसा है, दो kilometres दो हज़ार वाले notes जैसे, same value, ज़्यादा tidy.
और units convert करना factor-label method से होता है, एक fraction से गुणा करो जो one के बराबर हो, जैसे one kilogram बटा one thousand grams, ताकि unwanted unit cancel हो और wanted बच जाए।
दो ideas students को फँसाती हैं। Mass matter की amount है, kilograms में नापी जाती है, और कभी नहीं बदलती।
Weight उस mass पर gravitational force है, W बराबर m g, newton में नापी जाती है, और location के साथ बदलती है, mountaintop पर कम, Moon पर बहुत कम।
और temperature तीन scales में आती है, रोज़ के लिए Celsius, S I absolute scale Kelvin, और कुछ देशों में Fahrenheit.
एक rule पक्का याद रखो: Kelvin कभी negative नहीं होती। Negative kelvin temperature पक्का signal है कि कहीं error आ गई।

sections.title: The measurement toolkit

board_events.text: Core measurement relations
And $1\,\text{m}^3 = 10^{6}\,\text{cm}^3$ — cube the linear factor.
Celsius and Kelvin share degree size; only the offset 273.15 differs.

segments.text: Let's lay out the complete toolkit for this subtopic, the relations you will reach for in every numerical.
Density is mass over volume, its S I unit is kilogram per metre cubed, and the lab unit is gram per centimetre cubed.
For volume, one litre equals one thousand millilitres, equals one thousand centimetre cubed, equals ten to the minus three metre cubed.
And crucially, one metre cubed is ten to the sixth centimetre cubed, because you cube the linear factor, not square it.
For temperature, kelvin equals Celsius plus two seven three point one five.
Fahrenheit equals nine fifths of Celsius plus thirty two.
And going back, Celsius equals five ninths of the quantity Fahrenheit minus thirty two.
Weight is mass times g, where g is about nine point eight metre per second squared.
Notice why the temperature offsets look the way they do, Celsius and Kelvin share the same degree size, so only the offset of two seven three point one five separates them.
इस subtopic का पूरा toolkit रख देते हैं, वो relations जो हर numerical में काम आएँगी।
Density है mass बटा volume, इसकी S I unit kilogram per metre cubed है, और lab unit gram per centimetre cubed.
Volume के लिए, one litre बराबर one thousand millilitres, बराबर one thousand centimetre cubed, बराबर ten to the minus three metre cubed.
और सबसे ज़रूरी, one metre cubed है ten to the sixth centimetre cubed, क्योंकि linear factor को cube करते हो, square नहीं।
Temperature के लिए, kelvin बराबर Celsius plus two seven three point one five.
Fahrenheit बराबर nine fifths Celsius plus thirty two.
और वापस, Celsius बराबर five ninths, Fahrenheit minus thirty two का।
Weight है mass गुणा g, जहाँ g लगभग nine point eight metre per second squared है।
ध्यान दो temperature offsets ऐसे क्यों दिखते हैं, Celsius और Kelvin का degree size same है, इसलिए सिर्फ़ two seven three point one five का offset इन्हें अलग करता है।

sections.title: Temperature and prefix conversions

board_events.text: Body temperature 37 °C in K and °F
That is the familiar 98.6 of a thermometer.
Order by length: 1 nm, 1 µm, 1 pm, 1 mm
Compare exponents: pm 10⁻¹², nm 10⁻⁹, µm 10⁻⁶, mm 10⁻³.
Never rank by name; rank by the power of ten.

segments.text: Two quick conversions to build fluency. First, normal body temperature is thirty seven Celsius, express it in kelvin and Fahrenheit.
For kelvin, add two seven three point one five to thirty seven, giving three hundred ten point one five kelvin.
For Fahrenheit, nine fifths of thirty seven is sixty six point six, plus thirty two gives ninety eight point six Fahrenheit.
And there it is, the familiar ninety eight point six you read off a thermometer.
Second, arrange these four lengths in increasing order, one nanometre, one micrometre, one picometre, one millimetre.
Do not read the names, read the exponents. pico is ten to the minus twelve, nano minus nine, micro minus six, milli minus three.
So the order is picometre, then nanometre, then micrometre, then millimetre.
The trap is ranking by how familiar a name sounds. Always rank by the power of ten instead.
Fluency के लिए दो तेज़ conversions. पहला, normal body temperature thirty seven Celsius है, इसे kelvin और Fahrenheit में लिखो।
Kelvin के लिए, thirty seven में two seven three point one five जोड़ो, मिलता है three hundred ten point one five kelvin.
Fahrenheit के लिए, thirty seven का nine fifths है sixty six point six, plus thirty two देता है ninety eight point six Fahrenheit.
और यही है वो जाना पहचाना ninety eight point six जो thermometer पर पढ़ते हो।
दूसरा, इन चार lengths को बढ़ते क्रम में रखो, one nanometre, one micrometre, one picometre, one millimetre.
Names मत पढ़ो, exponents पढ़ो। pico है ten to the minus twelve, nano minus nine, micro minus six, milli minus three.
तो order है picometre, फिर nanometre, फिर micrometre, फिर millimetre.
Trap ये है कि name कितना जाना पहचाना लगता है उससे rank करना। हमेशा power of ten से rank करो।

sections.title: Density conversion and the cube trap

board_events.text: Mercury density 13.6 g cm⁻³ into SI
Mass of 250 mL: $m=\rho V = 13.6\times 250 = 3400\,\text{g} = 3.4\,\text{kg}$.
The cube factor is 10⁶, not 10² — that one step decides right vs wrong.
When do C and F read the SAME number?
Set the readings equal: let the common value be x.
So −40 °C equals −40 °F. Check: ⁹⁄₅(−40)+32 = −40.

segments.text: Now a J E E level density conversion, and a beautiful temperature puzzle.

Mercury has density thirteen point six gram per centimetre cubed. Convert grams to kilograms by dividing by one thousand, and centimetre cubed to metre cubed by multiplying by ten to the sixth, giving thirteen thousand six hundred kilogram per metre cubed.

For the mass of two hundred fifty millilitres, use density times volume in the original units, thirteen point six times two hundred fifty is three thousand four hundred grams, that is three point four kilograms.
Here is the step that separates right from wrong, the cube factor is ten to the sixth, not ten squared, because cubic units scale by the cube of the linear factor.
<curious>Now the puzzle. At what temperature do Celsius and Fahrenheit show the same number?
Same reading means set the two expressions equal. Let the common value be x.
So x equals nine fifths x plus thirty two. Bring terms together, minus four fifths x equals thirty two, which gives x equals minus forty.
So minus forty Celsius equals minus forty Fahrenheit, and the check confirms it, nine fifths of minus forty plus thirty two is indeed minus forty.
अब एक J E E level density conversion, और एक सुंदर temperature puzzle.

Mercury की density thirteen point six gram per centimetre cubed है। Grams को kilograms में करो one thousand से भाग देकर, और centimetre cubed को metre cubed में ten to the sixth से गुणा करके, मिलता है thirteen thousand six hundred kilogram per metre cubed.

Two hundred fifty millilitres के mass के लिए, original units में density गुणा volume लो, thirteen point six गुणा two hundred fifty है three thousand four hundred grams, यानी three point four kilograms.
यही वो step है जो सही और ग़लत को अलग करता है, cube factor ten to the sixth है, ten squared नहीं, क्योंकि cubic units linear factor के cube से scale होती हैं।
<curious>अब puzzle. किस temperature पर Celsius और Fahrenheit एक ही number दिखाते हैं?
Same reading का मतलब दोनों expressions को बराबर रखो। Common value को x मान लो।
तो x बराबर nine fifths x plus thirty two. Terms इकट्ठा करो, minus four fifths x बराबर thirty two, जिससे x बराबर minus forty.
तो minus forty Celsius बराबर minus forty Fahrenheit, और check confirm करता है, minus forty का nine fifths plus thirty two सचमुच minus forty है।

sections.title: Unit-handling pitfalls and the free error detector

board_events.text: Measurement pitfalls
Forgetting to cube or square the factor: $1\,\text{m}^3 = 10^{6}\,\text{cm}^3$, not 100.
Flipping the conversion factor: if the units don't cancel, the fraction is upside-down.
Use 273.15 (or 273 only when told to round); never report a negative kelvin.
Confusing mass and weight: mass (kg) is fixed, weight (N) depends on gravity.
Chemistry almost always deals with mass, not weight.
Pro-tip: carry units through the whole calculation — a free error detector.

segments.text: A short list of the slips that quietly sink correct-looking answers.
First, forgetting to cube or square the factor. One metre cubed is ten to the sixth centimetre cubed, not one hundred. Always raise the linear conversion to the power of the dimension.
Second, flipping the conversion factor. Set it so the unwanted unit cancels, and if the units do not cancel, your fraction is upside down.
Third, the temperature offset. Use two seven three point one five, or two seven three only when told to round, and never report a negative kelvin.
Fourth, confusing mass and weight. Mass in kilograms is fixed, while weight in newton depends on gravity.
And remember, chemistry almost always deals with mass, not weight, so keep that habit.

<excited>Here is the pro-tip that pays for itself: carry units through the entire calculation. If your final units do not simplify to what the answer should be, you made a mistake before you even checked the number.
उन slips की छोटी list जो सही दिखते answers को चुपचाप डुबा देती हैं।
पहला, factor को cube या square करना भूल जाना। One metre cubed है ten to the sixth centimetre cubed, one hundred नहीं। Linear conversion को हमेशा dimension की power तक उठाओ।
दूसरा, conversion factor उल्टा कर देना। इसे ऐसे रखो कि unwanted unit cancel हो, और अगर units cancel न हों, तो आपका fraction उल्टा है।
तीसरा, temperature offset. Two seven three point one five इस्तेमाल करो, या two seven three सिर्फ़ जब round करने को कहा जाए, और कभी negative kelvin मत लिखो।
चौथा, mass और weight को गड्डमड्ड करना। Mass kilograms में fixed है, जबकि weight newton में gravity पर depend करती है।
और याद रखो, chemistry लगभग हमेशा mass से deal करती है, weight से नहीं, तो ये आदत बनाए रखो।

<excited>अब वो pro-tip जो अपनी क़ीमत खुद वसूल करता है: units को पूरी calculation में साथ ले चलो। अगर final units वैसी नहीं simplify होतीं जैसी answer की होनी चाहिए, तो number check करने से पहले ही आपसे ग़लती हो गई।

sections.title: No measurement is exact: notation and significant figures

board_events.text: The last digit is always an estimate
Reading 2.5 cm off a ruler means 'close to 2.5' — the last digit is a guess.
Scientific notation: write as $N\times 10^{n}$ with $1\le N \lt 10$.
It saves ink and makes precision unambiguous — only the digits in N count.
Significant figures: the digits carrying real, reliable information.
Writing 12.50000 g from a coarse balance is a lie — false precision.
A count like '24 students' is exact: no estimated digit, infinite sig figs.
Defined relations like 1 m = 100 cm are exact too, and never limit a result.

segments.text: <curious>Here is a truth science is honest about, no measurement is ever exact.
When you read two point five centimetres off a ruler, you are really saying somewhere close to two point five. The last digit is always an estimate.
The first tool is scientific notation, writing any number as N times ten to the n, where N is between one and ten.
Beyond saving ink, it makes precision unambiguous, because only the digits in the coefficient N actually count.
Which brings us to the central idea, significant figures, the digits in a measurement that carry real, reliable information.
If a balance reads twelve point five grams, writing twelve point five zero zero zero zero would be a lie, you would be claiming a precision you do not have.
Now a crucial contrast. A count, like twenty four students, is exact, there is no estimated last digit, so it carries infinite significant figures and never limits a calculation.
The same is true of defined relations, like one metre equals one hundred centimetres. Distinguishing measured numbers from exact numbers is essential before any rule.
<curious>Science एक सच्चाई को ईमानदारी से मानती है, कोई measurement कभी exact नहीं होती।
जब आप ruler पर two point five centimetres पढ़ते हो, असल में कह रहे हो two point five के आसपास कहीं। Last digit हमेशा एक estimate है।
पहला tool है scientific notation, किसी भी number को N गुणा ten to the n लिखना, जहाँ N one और ten के बीच हो।
Ink बचाने के अलावा, ये precision को unambiguous बना देता है, क्योंकि सिर्फ़ coefficient N के digits ही count होते हैं।
यहीं से आता है central idea, significant figures, measurement के वो digits जो real, reliable information रखते हैं।
अगर balance twelve point five grams दिखाता है, तो twelve point five zero zero zero zero लिखना एक झूठ होगा, आप ऐसी precision claim कर रहे हो जो आपके पास है ही नहीं।
अब एक ज़रूरी contrast. एक count, जैसे twenty four students, exact है, कोई estimated last digit नहीं, तो ये infinite significant figures रखता है और calculation को कभी limit नहीं करता।
यही defined relations के साथ सच है, जैसे one metre बराबर one hundred centimetres. किसी भी rule से पहले measured numbers को exact numbers से अलग पहचानना ज़रूरी है।

sections.title: Accuracy vs precision, counting rules, and rounding

board_events.text: Accuracy vs precision
Accuracy: how close to the true value. Precision: how close repeated readings are to each other.
Archers: tight-but-off = precise; scattered-around-centre = accurate; tight-on-bull = both.
Non-zero digits count; captive zeros between non-zeros count.
Leading zeros never count; trailing zeros count only with a decimal point.
Rounding a lone 5: round-to-even — even stays, odd climbs.
Add/subtract: fewest decimal places. Multiply/divide: fewest significant figures.
Weakest link: the least precise input caps the whole calculation.

segments.text: Two words get muddled and deserve pinning down, accuracy and precision.
Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value. Precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other, regardless of the truth.
Picture three archers. One clusters tightly but off to the side, precise but not accurate. One scatters around the bullseye, accurate on average but not precise. The third clusters on the bull, both.
Now the counting rules. All non-zero digits are significant, and captive zeros sandwiched between non-zeros are significant too.
Leading zeros are just placeholders and never count, while trailing zeros count only when a decimal point is present.
For rounding when the dropped digit is exactly five, use round-to-even, leave an even digit unchanged and push an odd digit up by one.
For calculations, addition and subtraction keep the fewest decimal places, while multiplication and division keep the fewest significant figures.
The guiding principle behind all of it, a chain is only as strong as its weakest link, the least precise input caps the precision of the whole calculation.
दो शब्द अक्सर गड्डमड्ड होते हैं और साफ़ करने लायक़ हैं, accuracy और precision.
Accuracy है measurement true value के कितने पास है। Precision है repeated measurements एक दूसरे के कितने पास हैं, सच से बेपरवाह।
तीन archers सोचो। एक tight पर side में, precise पर accurate नहीं। एक bullseye के आसपास बिखरा, average में accurate पर precise नहीं। तीसरा bull पर tight, दोनों।
अब counting rules. सारे non-zero digits significant हैं, और non-zeros के बीच फँसे captive zeros भी significant हैं।
Leading zeros सिर्फ़ placeholders हैं और कभी count नहीं होते, जबकि trailing zeros तभी count होते हैं जब decimal point मौजूद हो।
जब dropped digit ठीक five हो तो rounding के लिए round-to-even इस्तेमाल करो, even digit वैसा ही रखो और odd digit को एक बढ़ा दो।
Calculations में, addition और subtraction सबसे कम decimal places रखते हैं, जबकि multiplication और division सबसे कम significant figures.
इन सबके पीछे guiding principle, एक chain उतनी ही मज़बूत जितनी उसकी सबसे कमज़ोर कड़ी, सबसे कम precise input पूरी calculation की precision को cap कर देता है।

sections.title: Counting, rounding, and combining figures

board_events.text: Count significant figures
Round to 3 significant figures
Sheet 2.1 cm × 3.46 cm: perimeter and area
Perimeter (decimals rule): $2\times 5.56 = 11.2$ cm, kept to 1 decimal.
Area (sig-fig rule): $2.1\times 3.46 = 7.266 \to 7.3$ cm² (2 sig figs).
Decimals govern the sum; significant figures govern the product.

segments.text: Let's drill counting, rounding and combining in one sweep. First, count the significant figures.

Zero point zero zero two five zero has three, one point zero zero four has four, fifty thousand with no decimal has just one, six point zero two two times ten to the twenty three has four, and one hundred point zero has four.
Second, round each to three significant figures, and watch the lone five.

Two point seven four five drops the five, the four before is even so it stays, giving two point seven four. Two point seven three five, the three is odd so it climbs, also two point seven four. And zero point zero two three four five six rounds to zero point zero two three five.
Third, a rectangular sheet two point one by three point four six centimetres, find perimeter and area, using both rules.
The perimeter is an addition, two times five point five six, but two point one has only one decimal place, so the answer is eleven point two centimetres.

The area is a multiplication, two point one times three point four six is seven point two six six, but two point one has only two significant figures, so the area is seven point three centimetre squared.
Notice the two rules pick different limiting terms, decimals govern the sum, while significant figures govern the product.
Counting, rounding और combining को एक साथ drill करते हैं। पहला, significant figures गिनो।

Zero point zero zero two five zero में three हैं, one point zero zero four में four, fifty thousand बिना decimal के सिर्फ़ one, six point zero two two गुणा ten to the twenty three में four, और one hundred point zero में four.
दूसरा, हर एक को three significant figures तक round करो, और lone five पर नज़र रखो।

Two point seven four five में five गिरता है, आगे वाला four even है तो वैसा रहता है, मिलता है two point seven four. Two point seven three five में three odd है तो चढ़ता है, फिर भी two point seven four. और zero point zero two three four five six round होकर zero point zero two three five.
तीसरा, एक rectangular sheet two point one गुणा three point four six centimetres, perimeter और area निकालो, दोनों rules से।
Perimeter एक addition है, two गुणा five point five six, पर two point one में सिर्फ़ one decimal place है, तो answer है eleven point two centimetres.

Area एक multiplication है, two point one गुणा three point four six है seven point two six six, पर two point one में सिर्फ़ two significant figures हैं, तो area है seven point three centimetre squared.
देखो दोनों rules अलग limiting term चुनते हैं, decimals sum को चलाते हैं, जबकि significant figures product को।

sections.title: Scientific-notation addition: align exponents first

board_events.text: Evaluate 4.5×10⁴ + 2.3×10³
First bring both terms to a common power of ten.
Now apply the addition rule to the coefficients at the common power.
4.5 has 1 decimal place, so the sum is limited to 1 decimal place.
Decide sig figs only AFTER aligning exponents — decimal places need a shared power of ten.

segments.text: A short J E E Advanced style problem that hides a subtlety. Evaluate four point five times ten to the four plus two point three times ten to the three.
The first move is to bring both terms to the same power of ten, otherwise decimal places are not comparable.
Rewriting the second term at ten to the four, four point five times ten to the four plus zero point two three times ten to the four equals four point seven three times ten to the four.
Now, and only now, apply the addition rule to the coefficients written at the common power.
Four point five has one decimal place while zero point two three has two, so the sum is limited to one decimal place.
That gives four point seven times ten to the four as the final answer.

Here is the subtlety worth remembering, decide the significant figures only after aligning the exponents, because decimal places only have a consistent meaning once both numbers share the same power of ten.
एक छोटा J E E Advanced style problem जिसमें एक subtlety छिपी है। Evaluate करो four point five गुणा ten to the four plus two point three गुणा ten to the three.
पहली चाल दोनों terms को एक ही power of ten पर लाना है, वरना decimal places comparable नहीं होते।
दूसरे term को ten to the four पर लिखो, four point five गुणा ten to the four plus zero point two three गुणा ten to the four बराबर four point seven three गुणा ten to the four.
अब, और सिर्फ़ अब, common power पर लिखे coefficients पर addition rule लगाओ।
Four point five में one decimal place है जबकि zero point two three में two, तो sum one decimal place तक limited है।
इससे मिलता है four point seven गुणा ten to the four, यही final answer.
यही subtlety याद रखने लायक़ है, significant figures तभी तय करो जब exponents align हो जाएँ, क्योंकि decimal places का consistent मतलब तभी बनता है जब दोनों numbers एक ही power of ten share करें।

sections.title: Sig-fig pitfalls and rounding once at the end

board_events.text: Significant-figure pitfalls
Mishandling zeros: leading never count; trailing count only with a decimal point.
Always rounding 5 up is wrong — use round-to-even.
Mixing the rules: sums follow decimals, products follow significant figures.
You can never be more precise than your least precise input.
Rounding at each step lets small errors snowball into a wrong final figure.
Pro-tip: carry guard digits through, round only once, at the very end.

segments.text: Four pitfalls and one habit that will keep your numbers honest.

First, mishandling zeros. Leading zeros never count, and trailing zeros count only when a decimal point is present, so zero point zero zero two five has two, but two thousand five hundred without a decimal has two as well.
Second, always rounding a five up. When the dropped digit is exactly five, use round-to-even, even stays, odd climbs.
Third, mixing the calculation rules. Sums and differences follow decimal places, while products and quotients follow significant figures. Using the wrong one is a classic slip.
Fourth, manufacturing precision. A result can never be more precise than its least precise input.
And beware step-by-step rounding, rounding at each stage lets small errors snowball into a wrong final figure.

<excited>So here is the pro-tip, carry one or two guard digits through every intermediate step, and round only once, at the very end. Ask which input was the weakest link, that input sets your figure count.
चार pitfalls और एक आदत जो आपके numbers को ईमानदार रखेगी।

पहला, zeros को ग़लत handle करना। Leading zeros कभी count नहीं होते, और trailing zeros तभी count होते हैं जब decimal point हो, तो zero point zero zero two five में two हैं, पर बिना decimal के two thousand five hundred में भी two.
दूसरा, five को हमेशा ऊपर round करना। जब dropped digit ठीक five हो, round-to-even इस्तेमाल करो, even रहता है, odd चढ़ता है।
तीसरा, calculation rules को mix करना। Sums और differences decimal places follow करते हैं, जबकि products और quotients significant figures. ग़लत वाला इस्तेमाल एक classic slip है।
चौथा, precision manufacture करना। कोई result अपने सबसे कम precise input से ज़्यादा precise कभी नहीं हो सकता।
और step-by-step rounding से बचो, हर stage पर round करने से छोटी errors snowball बनकर final figure ग़लत कर देती हैं।

<excited>तो ये है pro-tip, हर intermediate step में एक दो guard digits साथ ले चलो, और सिर्फ़ एक बार round करो, बिल्कुल अंत में। पूछो कौन सा input सबसे कमज़ोर कड़ी था, वही input आपकी figure count तय करता है।

sections.subtopic: Laws of Chemical Combination & Atomic Theory
sections.title: The five laws and the invisible bricks behind them

board_events.text: Nature combines in fixed, whole-number proportions
1. Conservation of mass: matter is only rearranged, never gained or lost.
2. Definite proportions: a compound has the same elements in the same fixed mass ratio.
3. Multiple proportions: two elements forming several compounds do so in small whole-number ratios.
4. Reciprocal proportions: how two elements combine with a third predicts how they combine with each other.
5. Combining volumes (gases): the same whole-number simplicity, now in volumes.
Dalton (1808): matter is identical bricks combining in fixed whole-number ratios.
The laws are the experimental footprints those invisible bricks leave behind.

segments.text: <curious>Picture your grandmother's secret masala, for every two spoons of cumin, exactly one of pepper, never a pinch more, in Chennai or Amritsar.
Nature is even stricter. The first law is conservation of mass, in a reaction nothing is gained or lost, matter is only rearranged.
Second, definite proportions, a given compound always contains the same elements in the same fixed proportion by mass.
Third, multiple proportions, when the same two elements form more than one compound, the numbers that appear are small whole numbers, never messy fractions.
Fourth, reciprocal proportions, the way two elements each combine with a third quietly predicts how they will combine with each other.
Fifth, Gay Lussac's law of combining volumes, for gases the same whole number simplicity appears, but now in volumes rather than masses.
Picture matter as identical L E G O bricks of fixed weight. John Dalton formalised exactly this in eighteen oh eight as his atomic theory.
And these five laws are precisely the experimental footprints those invisible bricks leave behind.
<curious>अपनी दादी का secret masala सोचो, हर दो spoon cumin पर ठीक एक pepper, एक चुटकी ज़्यादा नहीं, Chennai हो या Amritsar.
Nature तो और भी सख़्त है। पहला law है conservation of mass, reaction में कुछ न बनता न घटता, matter सिर्फ़ rearrange होता है।
दूसरा, definite proportions, कोई भी compound हमेशा एक ही elements को एक ही fixed proportion by mass में रखता है।
तीसरा, multiple proportions, जब वही दो elements एक से ज़्यादा compound बनाते हैं, तो जो numbers आते हैं वो small whole numbers होते हैं, कभी उलझे fractions नहीं।
चौथा, reciprocal proportions, दो elements जिस तरह किसी तीसरे से combine करते हैं वो चुपके से बता देता है कि वो आपस में कैसे combine करेंगे।
पाँचवाँ, Gay Lussac का law of combining volumes, gases के लिए वही whole number simplicity आती है, पर अब masses की जगह volumes में।
Matter को fixed weight वाले identical L E G O bricks समझो। John Dalton ने बिल्कुल यही eighteen oh eight में अपनी atomic theory के रूप में formalise किया।
और ये पाँचों laws ठीक वही experimental footprints हैं जो वो invisible bricks पीछे छोड़ते हैं।

sections.subtopic: Laws of Chemical Combination & Atomic Theory
sections.title: Avogadro's rescue: atom versus molecule

board_events.text: Gay-Lussac's paradox and Avogadro's fix
Gay-Lussac: 2 volumes H₂ + 1 volume O₂ → 2 volumes water vapour.
Dalton's indivisible atoms couldn't explain this without 'half an oxygen atom'.
Avogadro (1811): equal volumes of gases (same T, P) hold equal numbers of molecules.
Elemental gases like H₂, O₂, N₂ are diatomic — suddenly the ratios make sense.
Atom: smallest particle of an element. Molecule: smallest particle able to exist independently.
HCl evidence: 1 vol H₂ + 1 vol Cl₂ → 2 vol HCl, only if each molecule splits into atoms.
Running Avogadro backwards from volumes gives the atomicity of the gases.

segments.text: The story has a beautiful twist that taught chemistry a deep lesson.
Gay Lussac noticed gases combine in simple volume ratios, two volumes of hydrogen plus one volume of oxygen give two volumes of water vapour.
Dalton's indivisible atoms could not explain this cleanly, because two atoms plus one atom giving two particles would need half an oxygen atom, which he declared impossible.
In eighteen eleven Avogadro resolved it with one elegant idea, equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of molecules.
And elemental gases like hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen are diatomic. Suddenly the volume ratios made perfect sense.
This is where chemistry learned the crucial difference, an atom is the smallest particle of an element, a molecule is the smallest particle that can exist independently.

The cleanest evidence is hydrogen chloride, one volume of hydrogen plus one volume of chlorine gives two volumes, which is only possible if each molecule splits, so hydrogen and chlorine must be diatomic.
That same trick, running Avogadro's law backwards from measured volumes, is exactly how early chemists deduced the atomicity of the common gases.
इस कहानी में एक सुंदर twist है जिसने chemistry को एक गहरा सबक़ सिखाया।
Gay Lussac ने देखा कि gases simple volume ratios में combine होती हैं, दो volume hydrogen plus एक volume oxygen देते हैं दो volume water vapour.
Dalton के indivisible atoms इसे साफ़ explain नहीं कर पाए, क्योंकि दो atom plus एक atom से दो particle के लिए आधा oxygen atom चाहिए, जो उन्होंने असंभव बताया।
Eighteen eleven में Avogadro ने एक elegant idea से इसे हल किया, same temperature और pressure पर equal volumes of gases में equal number of molecules होते हैं।
और hydrogen, oxygen और nitrogen जैसी elemental gases diatomic हैं। अचानक volume ratios बिल्कुल सही बैठ गए।
यहीं chemistry ने ज़रूरी फ़र्क़ सीखा, atom किसी element का सबसे छोटा particle है, molecule वो सबसे छोटा particle जो अकेले मौजूद रह सके।
सबसे साफ़ evidence है hydrogen chloride, एक volume hydrogen plus एक volume chlorine देते हैं दो volume, जो तभी संभव है जब हर molecule टूटे, तो hydrogen और chlorine diatomic होने ही चाहिए।
यही चाल, Avogadro के law को measured volumes से उल्टा चलाना, ठीक वही तरीक़ा था जिससे शुरुआती chemists ने common gases की atomicity निकाली।

board_events.text: Multiple proportions: fix the common element to the same mass, then ratio the other.
Combining volumes: treat volumes like moles (Avogadro) and balance atoms.

segments.text: There is no algebra to derive these laws, so what exams test is the reverse skill, given a table of masses, decide which law it obeys. Start by counting.
If it is one reaction and you are comparing reactant mass against product mass, think conservation of mass.
If it is one compound analysed from several sources, think definite proportions.
If it is two different compounds made of the same two elements, think multiple proportions.
If three elements are interlinked through a common one, think reciprocal proportions, and if you are given volumes of gases, think combining volumes and Avogadro.
Here is that decision on one board, the trigger word is sitting inside the structure of the data itself.
For multiple proportions, the key step is to fix the common element to the same mass in both compounds first, and only then ratio the other element.
For combining volumes, treat the volumes exactly like moles, thanks to Avogadro, and balance atoms across the gaseous equation to extract an unknown formula.
इन laws को derive करने के लिए कोई algebra नहीं है, तो exams reverse skill test करते हैं, masses की table देकर तय करो कौन सा law है। शुरुआत गिनने से करो।
अगर एक reaction है और आप reactant mass को product mass से compare कर रहे हो, तो सोचो conservation of mass.
अगर एक compound कई sources से analyse हुआ है, तो सोचो definite proportions.
अगर वही दो elements से बने दो अलग compounds हैं, तो सोचो multiple proportions.
अगर तीन elements किसी एक common के ज़रिए जुड़े हैं, तो सोचो reciprocal proportions, और अगर gases के volumes दिए हैं, तो सोचो combining volumes और Avogadro.
ये रहा वो पूरा decision एक board पर, trigger word data की structure के अंदर ही बैठा है।
Multiple proportions के लिए, key step है common element को दोनों compounds में पहले same mass पर fix करना, और तभी दूसरे element का ratio निकालना।
Combining volumes के लिए, volumes को बिल्कुल moles की तरह treat करो, Avogadro की वजह से, और unknown formula निकालने के लिए gaseous equation में atoms balance करो।

sections.subtopic: Laws of Chemical Combination & Atomic Theory
sections.title: The five laws as precise statements

board_events.text: Statements of the laws of combination
Reciprocal: masses of A and B combining with a fixed mass of C give the A : B ratio.
Atomicity: He = 1, O₂ = 2, O₃ = 3.
Relative atomic mass: mass relative to ¹⁄₁₂ of a ¹²C atom (defined as exactly 12 u).

segments.text: Here are the laws stated precisely, the toolkit for every identify-the-law question.
Conservation of mass, from Lavoisier, the sum of reactant masses equals the sum of product masses, in a closed system.
Definite proportions, from Proust, the mass ratio of two elements is identical across any two samples of the same compound.
Multiple proportions, from Dalton, fixing the mass of one element, the masses of the other across two compounds form a small whole number ratio.
Reciprocal proportions, from Richter, the masses of A and B that each combine with a fixed mass of C give the ratio in which A and B combine directly.
Avogadro's law, volume is proportional to moles, so at the same temperature and pressure the ratio of volumes equals the ratio of moles.
Atomicity is the number of atoms in one molecule of an element, helium is one, oxygen gas is two, ozone is three.
And relative atomic mass is the mass of an atom relative to one twelfth of a carbon twelve atom, which is defined as exactly twelve units.
ये रहे laws precisely stated, हर identify-the-law सवाल का toolkit.
Conservation of mass, Lavoisier से, reactant masses का sum बराबर product masses का sum, closed system में।
Definite proportions, Proust से, एक ही compound के किन्हीं दो samples में दो elements का mass ratio एक जैसा रहता है।
Multiple proportions, Dalton से, एक element का mass fix करके, दो compounds में दूसरे element के masses small whole number ratio बनाते हैं।
Reciprocal proportions, Richter से, A और B के masses जो किसी fixed mass of C से combine होते हैं, वही ratio देते हैं जिसमें A और B सीधे combine करते हैं।
Avogadro का law, volume moles के proportional है, तो same temperature और pressure पर volumes का ratio moles के ratio के बराबर होता है।
Atomicity किसी element के एक molecule में atoms की संख्या है, helium एक, oxygen gas दो, ozone तीन।
और relative atomic mass किसी atom का mass है carbon twelve atom के one twelfth के relative, जो ठीक twelve units define किया गया है।

sections.subtopic: Laws of Chemical Combination & Atomic Theory
sections.title: Conservation of mass and multiple proportions

board_events.text: Fe + S in a sealed container
5.6 g iron + 3.2 g sulphur, sealed → closed system.
'Sealed container' is the marker for conservation of mass.
Two oxides of sulphur
Oxide A: 16 g S with 16 g O. Oxide B: 16 g S with 24 g O.
S already equalised → clean 2 : 3 → multiple proportions.

segments.text: Two examples that make the classification automatic. First, iron reacts with sulphur in a sealed, rigid container.
Five point six grams of iron reacts completely with three point two grams of sulphur, and because the container is sealed, it is a closed system.
By conservation of mass, the iron sulphide formed is simply the sum, eight point eight grams.
Notice the marker, the phrase sealed container is what tells you conservation of mass applies cleanly.
<chuckle>Second, sulphur forms two oxides, and we must name the law demonstrated.
In oxide A, sixteen grams of sulphur combines with sixteen grams of oxygen, and in oxide B, sixteen grams of sulphur combines with twenty four grams of oxygen.
The sulphur is already fixed at sixteen grams in both, so just ratio the oxygen, sixteen over twenty four is two to three.
A clean small whole number ratio like two to three means the law of multiple proportions, done in under ten seconds.
दो examples जो classification को automatic बना देते हैं। पहला, iron sulphur के साथ एक sealed, rigid container में react करता है।
पाँच point छह grams iron पूरी तरह तीन point दो grams sulphur से react करता है, और container sealed होने की वजह से ये closed system है।
Conservation of mass से, बना हुआ iron sulphide बस sum है, आठ point आठ grams.
Marker पर ध्यान दो, sealed container वाला phrase ही बताता है कि conservation of mass साफ़ लागू होता है।
<chuckle>दूसरा, sulphur दो oxides बनाता है, और हमें demonstrate हुआ law बताना है।
Oxide A में sixteen grams sulphur sixteen grams oxygen से combine होता है, और oxide B में sixteen grams sulphur twenty four grams oxygen से।
Sulphur दोनों में पहले से sixteen grams पर fixed है, तो बस oxygen का ratio निकालो, sixteen बटा twenty four है two to three.
Two to three जैसा clean small whole number ratio मतलब law of multiple proportions, दस second से भी कम में।

sections.subtopic: Laws of Chemical Combination & Atomic Theory
sections.title: Combining volumes and reciprocal proportions

board_events.text: Hydrocarbon by combining volumes (JEE Main)
1 vol CₓHᵧ + 5 vol O₂ → 3 vol CO₂ + 4 vol H₂O (same T, P).
Carbon: 3 CO₂ → x = 3. Hydrogen: 4 H₂O → y = 8.
O check: 3×2 + 4×1 = 10 atoms = 5 O₂ ✓
Reciprocal proportions via a bridge element
Per 1 g H: methane gives 3.00 g C; water gives 8.01 g O. Predicted C : O = 3.00 : 8.01.
CO₂ directly gives 27.3 : 72.7 = 3.00 : 8.00 — they agree.

segments.text: Now the two harder laws, tied to real problems. First, a J E E Main favourite on combining volumes.

One volume of a hydrocarbon burns in five volumes of oxygen to give three volumes of carbon dioxide and four volumes of water vapour, all at the same conditions. By Avogadro, volumes equal molecule ratios.
All carbon ends up in carbon dioxide, three molecules carry three carbon atoms, so x is three. All hydrogen ends up in water, four molecules carry eight hydrogen atoms, so y is eight.
That gives the hydrocarbon as C three H eight, propane.
And the sanity check confirms it, products hold three times two plus four times one, ten oxygen atoms, which is exactly the five oxygen molecules given.
<curious>Second, reciprocal proportions, verified through a bridge element, here hydrogen.

Fix one gram of hydrogen. From methane it combines with three point zero zero grams of carbon, from water with eight point zero one grams of oxygen, so carbon to oxygen is predicted as three to eight point zero one.

Now the direct test from carbon dioxide, twenty seven point three to seventy two point seven is three to eight point zero zero. The prediction and the observation agree, so reciprocal proportions holds.
अब दो कठिन laws, असली problems से जुड़े। पहला, combining volumes पर एक J E E Main favourite.
एक volume hydrocarbon पाँच volume oxygen में जलकर तीन volume carbon dioxide और चार volume water vapour देता है, सब same conditions पर। Avogadro से, volumes molecule ratios के बराबर हैं।
सारा carbon carbon dioxide में जाता है, तीन molecules तीन carbon atoms रखते हैं, तो x है तीन। सारा hydrogen water में जाता है, चार molecules आठ hydrogen atoms रखते हैं, तो y है आठ।
इससे hydrocarbon बनता है C three H eight, propane.
और sanity check confirm करता है, products रखते हैं तीन गुणा दो plus चार गुणा एक, दस oxygen atoms, जो ठीक दिए गए पाँच oxygen molecules हैं।
<curious>दूसरा, reciprocal proportions, एक bridge element से verify, यहाँ hydrogen.
एक gram hydrogen fix करो। Methane से ये तीन point zero zero grams carbon से combine होता है, water से आठ point zero one grams oxygen से, तो carbon to oxygen predicted है तीन to आठ point zero one.
अब carbon dioxide से direct test, twenty seven point three to seventy two point seven है तीन to आठ point zero zero. Prediction और observation मेल खाते हैं, तो reciprocal proportions सही है।

sections.subtopic: Laws of Chemical Combination & Atomic Theory
sections.title: Law pitfalls and the five-second classifier

board_events.text: Pitfalls with the laws of combination
Open system ≠ broken law: a burning candle loses apparent mass only because gases escape.
Multiple proportions: never compare total masses; fix the common element first.
Gas volumes are molecule ratios (Avogadro), not mass ratios — don't convert to grams.
Dalton's cracks: isotopes differ in mass; the atom is divisible.
Dalton's 'conserved in reactions' still holds for chemical reactions — not the false postulate.
Pro-tip: count compounds and elements before touching any number.

segments.text: Four traps and one habit that make identify-the-law questions almost free.
First, mistaking an open system for a broken law. A burning candle appears to lose mass, but only because carbon dioxide and water vapour escape, mass is fully conserved.
Second, comparing the wrong quantities in multiple proportions. Students compare total masses or forget to equalise the fixed element, always fix the common element to the same value first.
Third, treating gas volumes as masses. Volume ratios are molecule ratios via Avogadro, so do not convert to grams unless the question asks.
Fourth, over-applying Dalton. Remember the modern cracks, isotopes are atoms of one element with different masses, and the atom is divisible into subatomic particles.
But note, Dalton's claim that atoms are conserved in chemical reactions still holds, so it is not the incorrect postulate in those tricky questions.
<excited>And here is the pro-tip, before touching any number, count how many compounds and how many elements the data describes. That five second classification alone earns the mark.
चार traps और एक आदत जो identify-the-law सवालों को लगभग मुफ़्त बना देती है।
पहला, open system को broken law समझना। जलती हुई candle mass खोती दिखती है, पर सिर्फ़ इसलिए कि carbon dioxide और water vapour निकल जाते हैं, mass पूरी तरह conserved है।
दूसरा, multiple proportions में ग़लत quantities compare करना। Students total masses compare करते हैं या fixed element equalise करना भूल जाते हैं, हमेशा common element को पहले same value पर fix करो।
तीसरा, gas volumes को masses मानना। Volume ratios Avogadro से molecule ratios हैं, तो जब तक सवाल न कहे grams में मत बदलो।
चौथा, Dalton को ज़्यादा apply करना। Modern cracks याद रखो, isotopes एक element के atoms हैं अलग masses के साथ, और atom subatomic particles में divisible है।
पर ध्यान दो, Dalton का ये claim कि atoms chemical reactions में conserved होते हैं अब भी सही है, तो उन tricky सवालों में वो incorrect postulate नहीं है।
<excited>और ये है pro-tip, कोई number छूने से पहले गिनो data कितने compounds और कितने elements बताता है। वो पाँच second का classification अकेले ही mark दिला देता है।

sections.title: The mole: a chemist's dozen

board_events.text: One mole = 6.022×10²³ entities
We count atoms in batches, exactly as we buy eggs by the dozen.
One mole of anything is 6.022×10²³ of it — marbles would bury Earth; molecules fit in a spoon.
Genius of the choice: mass of one mole (in grams) = the relative atomic mass numerically.
Carbon (12) → 12 g per mole; oxygen (16) → 16 g per mole.
So weigh 12 g of carbon and you have, without counting, 6.022×10²³ atoms.
The mole bridges single atoms (in u) to the laboratory balance (in grams).

segments.text: <curious>When you buy eggs you do not count them one by one, you ask for a dozen. Atoms push this idea to its extreme.
A single grain of sand holds more atoms than there are grains of sand on every beach in India, so chemists invented their own dozen and called it the mole.
A mole is a fixed, agreed number of things, Avogadro's number, six point zero two two times ten to the twenty three.
One mole of anything is that many of it. One mole of marbles would bury the Earth, one mole of molecules fits in a spoon, and that gap is the whole point.
Here is the genius of the choice. The mole was defined so the mass of one mole of an element, in grams, equals its relative atomic mass numerically.
Carbon has relative atomic mass twelve, so one mole of carbon weighs twelve grams. Oxygen, sixteen, gives sixteen grams per mole.
So weigh out twelve grams of carbon and you have, without ever counting, exactly six point zero two two times ten to the twenty three atoms.
That is the bridge chemistry needed, connecting single atoms measured in units to the laboratory balance measured in grams.
<curious>जब आप eggs ख़रीदते हो तो एक एक करके नहीं गिनते, एक dozen माँगते हो। Atoms इस idea को चरम तक ले जाते हैं।
रेत के एक कण में भारत के हर beach के रेत के कणों से ज़्यादा atoms होते हैं, तो chemists ने अपना dozen बनाया और उसे mole कहा।
Mole चीज़ों की एक fixed, तय संख्या है, Avogadro's number, six point zero two two times ten to the twenty three.
किसी भी चीज़ का एक mole उतना ही होता है। एक mole marbles पूरी Earth दबा देगी, एक mole molecules एक चम्मच में आ जाएँगी, और यही gap पूरी बात है।
अब choice की genius. Mole ऐसे define हुआ कि किसी element के एक mole का mass, grams में, उसके relative atomic mass के numerically बराबर हो।
Carbon का relative atomic mass twelve है, तो एक mole carbon का mass twelve grams. Oxygen, sixteen, देता है sixteen grams per mole.
तो twelve grams carbon तौल लो और आपके पास, बिना गिने, ठीक six point zero two two times ten to the twenty three atoms हैं।
यही वो bridge है जो chemistry को चाहिए था, units में नापे single atoms को grams में नापे laboratory balance से जोड़ता है।

sections.title: Relative and average atomic mass

board_events.text: Why chlorine's mass is 35.5, not a whole number
Atomic masses are measured relative to ¹⁄₁₂ of a carbon-12 atom = 1 u.
1 u ≈ 1.66×10⁻²⁴ g — far tidier than writing tiny gram values.
No chlorine atom actually weighs 35.5 u.
Chlorine is a mix of ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl in roughly 3 : 1 abundance.
35.5 is a weighted average — like a batting average, not any single innings.
The periodic-table value is the real-world isotopic average.
Never use an average mass as a single-atom mass in a nuclear context.

segments.text: <curious>Why is chlorine's atomic mass thirty five point five, and not a clean whole number?
First, we do not weigh atoms in grams, the numbers would be absurd. We measure relative to a reference, one twelfth of a carbon twelve atom defined as one unit.
That one unit is about one point six six times ten to the minus twenty four grams, far tidier than writing such tiny gram values every time.
Now the answer, no chlorine atom actually weighs thirty five point five units.
In nature, chlorine is a mixture of chlorine thirty five and chlorine thirty seven, in roughly three to one abundance.
So thirty five point five is a weighted average, exactly like a batsman's average is not the score of any single innings but the weighted result of all of them.
The value you read on the periodic table is precisely this real world isotopic average.
And a caution follows, never treat that average as the mass of a single atom in a nuclear context, no real atom has it.
<curious>Chlorine का atomic mass thirty five point five क्यों है, कोई साफ़ whole number क्यों नहीं?
पहले, हम atoms को grams में नहीं तौलते, numbers बेतुके हो जाएँगे। हम एक reference के relative नापते हैं, carbon twelve atom का one twelfth जिसे one unit define किया गया।
वो one unit लगभग one point six six times ten to the minus twenty four grams है, हर बार इतनी tiny gram values लिखने से कहीं tidier.
अब answer, कोई chlorine atom असल में thirty five point five units का नहीं होता।
प्रकृति में chlorine, chlorine thirty five और chlorine thirty seven का mixture है, लगभग three to one abundance में।
तो thirty five point five एक weighted average है, बिल्कुल जैसे batsman का average किसी एक innings का score नहीं बल्कि सबका weighted result होता है।
Periodic table पर जो value पढ़ते हो वो ठीक यही real world isotopic average है।
और एक caution, उस average को nuclear context में किसी single atom का mass कभी मत मानो, किसी असली atom का वो mass नहीं है।

sections.title: Molecular mass, formula mass, and vapour density in use

board_events.text: From atomic masses to a molecule's mass
Molecular mass = sum of atomic masses of all atoms in the molecule.
Formula mass: the same sum for an ionic formula unit like NaCl (no discrete molecule).
e.g. O₂: 2×16 = 32; recall atomicity from the laws subtopic.
Vapour density gives molar mass fast: measure V.D., then M = 2 × V.D.
Combine with M = atomicity × M_atomic to find an unknown gas's atomicity.

segments.text: Let's close the mole concept by turning atomic masses into the mass of a whole molecule.
The molecular mass is simply the sum of the atomic masses of every atom in the molecule.
For ionic solids there is no discrete molecule, so we use the formula mass, the same sum taken over one formula unit, like sodium chloride.
For an elemental gas, the molecular mass is the atomicity times the atomic mass.
For example, oxygen gas is two times sixteen, giving thirty two, and you recall the atomicity from the laws subtopic.
Vapour density gives the molar mass quickly, measure the vapour density and molar mass is just twice it.
So molar mass equals two times vapour density, because vapour density is defined relative to hydrogen gas, whose molar mass is about two.
Combine that with molar mass equals atomicity times atomic mass, and you can pin down the atomicity of an unknown elemental gas.
Mole concept को बंद करते हैं atomic masses को पूरे molecule के mass में बदलकर।
Molecular mass बस molecule के हर atom के atomic masses का sum है।
Ionic solids में कोई discrete molecule नहीं होता, तो हम formula mass इस्तेमाल करते हैं, वही sum एक formula unit पर लिया, जैसे sodium chloride.
किसी elemental gas के लिए, molecular mass है atomicity गुणा atomic mass.
उदाहरण के लिए, oxygen gas है two गुणा sixteen, यानी thirty two, और atomicity आप laws subtopic से याद करते हो।
Vapour density molar mass तेज़ी से देती है, vapour density नापो और molar mass बस उसका दुगना है।
तो molar mass बराबर two गुणा vapour density, क्योंकि vapour density hydrogen gas के relative define होती है, जिसका molar mass लगभग two है।
इसे molar mass बराबर atomicity गुणा atomic mass के साथ जोड़ो, और आप किसी unknown elemental gas की atomicity पक्की कर सकते हो।
